The Ramcarat grenadier anchovy (Coilia ramcarati) attains a maximum recorded adult body length of 25 centimeters [Li = 25 centimeters], a value documented from extensive trawl surveys in estuarine habitats of the northern Bay of Bengal. Morphometric analyses of preserved museum specimens indicate that sexual maturation occurs at a total length of 17.9 centimeters [Lp = 17.9 centimeters], a developmental landmark linked to the onset of gonadal recrudescence in this small pelagic clupeiform. The length-weight relationship derived from field-collected individuals follows the form W = 0.00380L^3.06, from which the estimated wet weight at puberty is calculated to be 26 grams [Wwp = 26 grams]. This relatively modest mass at maturity, consistent with values reported for other Coilia species, suggests a life-history strategy favoring early reproductive investment over extended somatic growth. Comparisons with congeneric taxa reveal that the ultimate body size of Coilia ramcarati overlaps considerably with that of the closely related Bombay duck (Harpadon nehereus), though the anchovy's more slender body form yields a lower asymptotic mass for a given length increment.

Reproductive output in Coilia ramcarati has been characterized under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 28.7 °C [T = 28.7 °C]. The maximum daily reproductive rate reaches approximately 58 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 58 eggs per day], a value derived from the observation that each female can produce an average of 58.4 eggs per day. This remarkably high daily fecundity, exceeding that reported for most other engraulids of comparable body size, reflects a rapid oocyte maturation cycle typical of tropical estuarine species with extended spawning seasons. The total annual reproductive output thus approximates 21334 eggs per year [Ri = 21334 eggs per year], a value that underscores the species' capacity for population resilience under favorable environmental conditions. Histological examination of ovarian tissue from gravid individuals confirmed the presence of asynchronous oocyte development, permitting continuous batch spawning throughout the warm monsoon months. The thermal regime appears optimal for sustaining this elevated reproductive tempo.

Eggs of Coilia ramcarati are spherical, transparent, and pelagic, with an average diameter of 0.8 millimeters. The resulting wet weight at birth for a newly fertilized ovum is estimated at 0.00027 grams [Wwb = estimated at 0.00027 grams], a minimal mass that is characteristic of planktonic fish eggs relying entirely on endogenous yolk reserves. At the same incubation temperature of 28.7 °C [T = 28.7 °C], embryonic development proceeds rapidly, with hatching occurring after just 5 days [ab = 5 days]. This brief period of embryogenesis is typical of tropical marine teleosts and reflects the accelerated developmental rates conferred by warm thermal conditions. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva measures approximately 2.5 millimeters in standard length and remains entirely lecithotrophic for the first 48 hours, relying on the residual yolk mass before the onset of exogenous feeding. Field observations indicate that larval survival during this critical window is heavily influenced by prey availability and water column stability in the spawning grounds.

Under the same stable thermal conditions of 28.7 °C [T = 28.7 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan for Coilia ramcarati is 5 years [am = 5 years], a duration typical of small, short-lived clupeiform fishes. Annulus counts from otolith sagittae collected during fishery-independent surveys confirm that mortality rates increase sharply after the third year, with very few individuals surviving beyond 1,825 days. This comparatively short life span, coupled with the extremely high reproductive output, positions Coilia ramcarati as an opportunistic strategist that capitalizes on seasonal productivity pulses in its estuarine habitat. The ultimate wet weight corresponding to the maximum length of 25 centimeters is 72 grams [Wwi = 72 grams], as derived from the species-specific length-weight conversion. This asymptotic body mass is modest even by anchovy standards, reflecting the streamlined, energy-efficient body plan that facilitates rapid growth during the juvenile phase.

Field mark-recapture studies have provided further insight into the growth trajectory of Coilia ramcarati, with individuals reaching 72 grams [Wwi = 72 grams] only after approximately three years of sustained feeding in productive deltaic ecosystems. The length at which 50% of individuals are reproductively mature remains consistently near 17.9 centimeters [Lp = 17.9 centimeters] across the species' geographic range. Teleost life-history theory predicts that such an early maturation relative to ultimate size, coupled with a 5-year lifespan (5 years) [am = 5 years] under the ambient temperature of 28.7 °C [T = 28.7 °C], should favor high reproductive effort in the first spawning season. The wet weight at birth of 0.00027 grams [Wwb = 0.00027 grams] represents an extreme reduction in propagule mass that is compensated by the elevated fecundity documented above. Comparative data from Coilia dussumieri suggest that this suite of traits has been evolutionarily conserved within the genus, reinforcing the pattern of small body size, early maturity, and prodigious egg production.
